h-sequence.name: The sequence, start to finish
h-sequence.teaser: Cold hall, hot marble, scrub, foam, rinse: ninety minutes to two hours, and nothing planned after
h-sequence.story: In the camekân, the cold domed hall, you take a numbered key and a cabin, strip and wrap. Then the hararet: you lie on the göbek taşı, the marble platform heated from below, until you sweat properly, because the scrub fails on cold skin. Only then does the attendant come with the kese, a coarse mitt that lifts dead skin in grey rolls. Foam follows, poured from a cloth bag, then hair, then rinsing with a bowl from the kurna, the basin you never climb into. You finish wrapped in dry cotton with tea. There is no sauna and no pool: Ottoman bathing never had either.
h-sequence.why: Know the order before you undress: at the busy restored houses nobody walks you through it unless you ask.
facts: Ninety minutes to two hours; Süleymaniye runs a fixed 1h45 (15 arriving, 30 on the marble, 30 scrub and soap, 30 cooling)
38–40°C at 65–72% humidity at Süleymaniye; Hürrem Sultan states 42°C on the platform and 48°C in its private rooms
A peştemal from waist to knee at least, over underwear or a bikini bottom; full nudity is forbidden at Kılıç Ali Paşa and Galatasaray. Women: bring a top too and follow the room
Peştemal, towel and slippers at every house here; Süleymaniye lends swimwear, Zeyrek keeps disposable underwear; items are for use on the premises only

A full or empty stomach, alcohol beforehand, a kese after a day in the sun; food and drink in the wet rooms

h-gender.name: Gendered hours — the way this trip actually fails
h-gender.teaser: Nine houses, four systems, two that never say which half runs when. Get it wrong and the door is locked
h-gender.story: Istanbul has no single rule. Some baths are çifte, twin buildings with a men's half and a women's half behind separate street doors. Some are one bath sliced by the clock, with a dead changeover between. Two are mixed and take any party of men and women together. Two describe separate sections yet publish one undifferentiated hours line. Two traps bite hardest: the last reservation is often hours before closing, and third-party listings lag behind the houses' own pages. A woman reaching Kılıç Ali Paşa at five in the afternoon does not get in; a man arriving there at eleven in the morning is turned away too.
h-gender.why: Phone the house the morning you go: the closing time on the door is not the time you can still walk in.

h-money.name: The money, the extras, and who is refused
h-money.teaser: The massage is never in the bath price, cash beats card, and some houses turn guests away at the door
h-money.story: The bath price has never included an oil massage. Kılıç Ali Paşa and Galatasaray say so in writing: a massage means a separate room, therapist, booking and bill, and at Kılıç Ali Paşa it costs more than the ritual itself. Expect it offered warmly while you are wet, wrapped and in no position to haggle. Decide before you go in, ask for the all-in total rather than the door price, and separate your tip notes before you undress. The houses also take medicine seriously: this is a room near 40°C and 70% humidity with a stranger pressing on you for half an hour, and some will refuse you.
h-money.why: Settle the total and the tip at the desk, dry and dressed; done later, in a wrap, it always costs more.

h-kilic-ali.name: Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı
h-kilic-ali.teaser: Sinan's bath for the crews of the Ottoman fleet: one dome, no second wing, and the clock decides who enters
h-kilic-ali.story: Mimar Sinan built this bath in the late 1570s inside admiral Kılıç Ali Pasha's mosque complex for the levends, the crews of the Ottoman fleet, when Tophane was the working harbour. The patron was born Giovanni Dionigi Galeni in Calabria, set to the oars as a galley slave, converted and rose to command the navy; Cervantes calls him Uchali. The hot room is one great volume under a dome fourteen metres wide and seventeen high, the house says the city's second-largest. Seven years of restoration ended in 2012, and Europa Nostra honoured it in 2017. There is no second wing: one bath, alternating by the clock.
h-kilic-ali.why: The best first hammam: one great dome and a ritual the house documents step by illustrated step.
facts: Kemankeş Mah., Hamam Sok. No:1, Tophane, Karaköy, Beyoğlu
Daily from 16:30 or 16:45 (the house gives both) to 23:30, last reservation 22:00 (seen Aug 2026)

h-zeyrek.name: Zeyrek Çinili Hamam
h-zeyrek.teaser: The grand admiral's bath, back in service after thirteen years of restoration, with a museum under the marble
h-zeyrek.story: Barbaros Hayreddin Paşa, grand admiral of the Ottoman fleet, commissioned it, and the house credits Mimar Sinan, building over a Byzantine cistern under Süleyman the Magnificent. The İznik tiles that named it left long ago for European collections. After a thirteen-year restoration under The Marmara Group it reopened in September 2023, and it is a museum as well as a bath: in the cistern below the women's cold room, plaster carries incised graffiti of galleys whose makers and date nobody knows. Every treatment ends back in the cold room with a rose-geranium towel for the face, Turkish tea and something sweet and savoury.
h-zeyrek.why: Go for the cistern graffiti and the polished dome; take The DIY if you would rather not be handled.

h-cagaloglu.name: Cağaloğlu Hamamı
h-cagaloglu.teaser: The last great bath the empire built in the city, and it was built to pay for a library
h-cagaloglu.story: Built in 1741 under Mahmud I, begun by the architect Süleyman Ağa and finished by Abdullah Ağa, it was endowed as a çifte bath to fund the sultan's library inside Hagia Sophia: the bath paid for the books. The house calls it the last of its kind built in Istanbul. Men climb ten steps between two marble columns with stalactite capitals, under an inscription of seven lines and twenty-eight verses; the steps exist because the street rose over three centuries. Inside the men's camekân a high dome with a lantern at its crown stands over a pool and a water jet. Women enter from another street entirely.
h-cagaloglu.why: Choose it for the 1741 architecture and lunch in the same building; the room itself is almost all visitors.
facts: Alemdar Mah., Prof. Kazım İsmail Gürkan Cad. No:34, Fatih

h-suleymaniye.name: Süleymaniye Hamamı
h-suleymaniye.teaser: Oak-fired around the clock, and the bath where a mixed party of men and women goes in through one door
h-suleymaniye.story: The house trades on 'Since 1550' and credits Mimar Sinan, though its own FAQ arithmetic lands nearer 1554. Two things set it apart. The first is the furnace: oak fires burn under the floor day and night, holding the hot room at 38 to 40°C. The second is the format. In its main session it takes mixed parties, any party of men and women together, family included, in one shared communal room, and it will not separate them: scrub and soap massage are taken side by side beside the kurna. The house page read in August said every tellak is male, for every guest, women included.
h-suleymaniye.why: The one bath where a mixed party bathes together; read the booking rules before you commit a day off.

h-aga.name: Ağa Hamamı
h-aga.teaser: Mixed, priced in lira, itemised line by line, and well under the Sultanahmet houses for the same three things
h-aga.story: A small bath in the Çukurcuma streets below Galatasaray, with the plainest pricing in the city: entrance, scrub and foam listed as three numbers you add up yourself, card and cash totals side by side. It is mixed, as it has been for over a decade by its own account, and it says plainly that it serves only tourists. The hot room holds the göbek taşı, with two small halvet chambers of three kurnas each, the hottest corners of the house, and a cold halvet to recover in. The külhan still burns wood, where most Istanbul baths now run on natural gas.
h-aga.why: The lowest published door price in Istanbul, and the only lira-priced house that keeps men and women of one group together.

h-uskudar.name: Tarihi Üsküdar Çinili Hamamı
h-uskudar.teaser: 1640, two-metre walls, a tonne of firewood a winter, cash only, and nobody explaining anything in English
h-uskudar.story: Built in 1640 for Kösem Sultan as one of four buildings in her Çinili complex, its first job was washing the masons raising the Çinili mosque. The house says Kösem died once the women's section was finished and her brother saw the rest through. The İznik tiles were stolen long ago; blue stone stands in for them. The walls are two metres thick, one kazan under the floor between the domes burns about a tonne of firewood over a winter, and when it gets too hot the old glass fanuslar are lifted out of the domes to vent. The marble carvings and kurnas are original.
h-uskudar.why: The one bath on this list that is selling nothing: neighbourhood marble, and very likely you the only foreigner on it.

r-tiras.name: Tıraş — the full berber
r-tiras.teaser: Cut, cut-throat shave, ear-singe, cologne: a licensed trade, with a printed tariff you may ask to see
r-tiras.story: The berber is a licensed trade with its own chamber, and licensed shops display a tarife, so asking to see the price list is normal here. The full saç sakal runs haircut, hot towel, brush lather, then the ustura, the open razor, with the grain and against it. A flame flicks over the ears to take the fine hair; it lasts two seconds and does not hurt. Alum on the nicks, a second towel, then lemon cologne poured into your cupped hands. Behind Hagia Sophia, Rimedzo has kept the same doorway since 1986 and tells you to read its list before you sit.
r-tiras.why: Forty-five minutes in the chair is the most Istanbul thing a man can do for the price of lunch.
facts: Cut, open-razor shave, ear singe, cologne, then a glass of çay at the mirror
Forty-five minutes to an hour for saç sakal

r-2a-berber.name: 2.a Berber Barbershop
r-2a-berber.teaser: A shop above Karaköy that sells the cut-throat wet shave as its trade, and will come to the boat
r-2a-berber.story: Most Istanbul shops will shave you with an open razor if asked; this one sells it as the thing it does, calling itself one of the few places in the city offering a professional hot-towel, cut-throat shave. It sits on a side street on the slope above Karaköy and prints its prices in lira with euro and dollar beside them, which says who walks in. Hot towel, brush lather, razor, towel again, cologne. The detail for anyone working a yacht: by prior arrangement they come to you, to a flat or premises, and cut a whole crew in one go.
r-2a-berber.why: Book the call-out and the whole crew is shaved before the guests come aboard.
facts: Haircut 800 ₺, shave 500 ₺, cut and shave 1,200 ₺, beard shaping 700 ₺, on a page marked © 2021 (seen Aug 2026); check the board inside

r-sema.name: Sema — ceremony or show
r-sema.teaser: The tall felt hat and the white skirt appear at every tier. The costume never tells you what you bought
r-sema.story: UNESCO proclaimed the Mevlevi Sema a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008. What is protected is the ayin, a fixed four-part musical form for voice, ney, kudüm drum and cymbals, and the turn itself: left foot planted, right palm up to receive, left palm down to give. The Republic closed every tekke in 1925, and what survived of the order survived as culture on a stage, so the blur between rite and show is the price of its survival. The useful test is the room: a theatre with a foyer, or a hall where people also pray.
r-sema.why: Decide which you want, prayer or performance, and buy that honestly; both are worth an evening.
facts: A foundation's own ayin with no ticket desk; a ticketed sema in a real semahane such as Galata; a purpose-built show in a culture centre, such as Hodjapasha in Sirkeci (unconfirmed as running)
Whirling sold with dinner and belly dancing is the bottom tier, whatever the poster says
No applause and no flash, do not leave while they turn; long sleeves and trousers, women cover the head at a foundation, shoes off on a prayer floor
Deliberately not quoted: check the seller's own page on the day
The Saturday evening at the Silivrikapı foundation, or the Galata lodge's semahane by daylight

r-emav.name: Silivrikapı Mevlana Kültür Merkezi (EMAV)
r-emav.teaser: A foundation's own sema twice a week, the discourse subtitled in English, no ticket desk: phone for the door
r-emav.story: Evrensel Mevlana Aşıkları Vakfı runs its own weekly evenings at the Silivrikapı Mevlana Cultural Center, the house associated with Hasan Dede, who spent his life teaching there. For a non-Turkish speaker the rare thing is that the opening discourse is a recorded video with English subtitles, so you follow the evening rather than merely watch it. Partway through comes the ikram, food and drink offered to everyone sitting on the floor: the sign that you are a guest at somebody's evening, not an audience. Arrive for the start; slipping in at the end to catch the turning is what everyone notices.
r-emav.why: The closest a visitor gets to the rite itself, with subtitles, and it asks nothing at the door.
facts: Thursday 19:30–22:30, sema from 21:40; Saturday 19:00–20:30, sema from 19:50 (seen Aug 2026); moves for religious dates
The foundation names the Silivrikapı hall but prints no street address, only its Şehremini office: phone before you set out
No admission published; carry cash for a donation
Long sleeves and trousers, women cover the head, shoes off; you sit on the floor

r-galata-mevlevi.name: Galata Mevlevihanesi
r-galata-mevlevi.teaser: A 1491 lodge with a genuine semahane: visit it as a museum, and treat the ceremony as a maybe
r-galata-mevlevi.story: Founded in 1491 and known in Ottoman times as the Kulekapısı lodge, this is the one place a visitor can stand inside a real semahane on an ordinary weekday. It closed with every tekke in 1925, reopened as a museum in 1975 and was reorganised as the Mevlevi lodge museum in 2011. The hall is the reason: a wooden floor, mihrab and minber at the far end, the gallery where the musicians sat. Side rooms hold marbling, calligraphy and hilye sheets, and the courtyard holds the tomb of the poet Şeyh Galib, once sheikh here. It crowns Galip Dede Caddesi, the instrument-makers' street.
r-galata-mevlevi.why: Walk up from Karaköy past the instrument shops and have the semahane almost to yourself.

r-cay.name: Çay bahçesi — the price of a chair
r-cay.teaser: One glass of tea buys the table for as long as you want it. That is the whole contract, and it holds
r-cay.story: Law 407 of 1924 put tea growing on a legal footing at Rize on the wet Black Sea coast, to bring work to the east after the First World War; the first large harvest came in 1938, the first factory in 1947. Within a generation the glass ran the whole day. In a çay bahçesi one glass buys the table for as long as you like. It comes thin-waisted on a saucer with two sugar cubes, poured from a stacked double pot, brew above and hot water below, mixed to your order. Grandparents hold tables for four hours over backgammon. Nobody is moved on.
r-cay.why: A few small glasses rent you a view for the whole afternoon.
facts: 'Bir çay' for one, 'iki çay' for a pair; açık for pale, koyu for dark; refills one glass at a time
Sit anywhere free, a waiter with a tray finds you; pay at the end, often in cash
Tea, Turkish coffee and little else, no music, and your own food welcome
No milk; round up rather than tip; share the table when asked, not the conversation; refusing an offered glass is close to rude

r-nargile.name: Nargile — the medrese and the Tophane strip
r-nargile.teaser: If the pipe arrives in under ten minutes it was not built for you. The whole point is the two hours
r-nargile.story: Nargile reached Ottoman Istanbul in the seventeenth century, and Murad IV banned it alongside coffee and tobacco on the reasoning that men who sit together talk. Most of what is smoked now is mu'assel, tobacco cut with molasses and fruit; the older tömbeki, plain soaked leaf under raw coal, is harsher and slower, and still served if you ask for it by name. In the medrese Çorlulu Ali Paşa built in 1708 on the old Divanyolu, two courtyards of carpet dealers hold one of the city's long-standing nargile gardens: low stools, cushions, and a boy with tongs working the coals.
r-nargile.why: The cheapest way in the city to hold a table for a whole evening, if you accept what you are smoking.
facts: Çorlulu Ali Paşa Medresesi, Yeniçeriler Cad., Beyazıt, between the Grand Bazaar and Çemberlitaş; or the Tophane strip below İstiklal, where shop names turn over fast
'Nargile' and a flavour, or simply 'elma', apple; 'köz alabilir miyim?' for fresh coals
Not quoted: ask before the pipe is packed; the medrese is visitor-priced, Tophane runs at neighbourhood rates
A coal boy on the floor with tongs and a brazier, not a waiter with a lighter
Pass the hose by the stem; never light a cigarette from the coal; expect no alcohol
This is tobacco smoked for an hour or two; the water does not make it mild

r-kahve.name: Türk kahvesi — the cup, and the cup turned over
r-kahve.teaser: One small cup, twenty minutes, a foam you judge it by, and the grounds left for a stranger to read
r-kahve.story: Hakem of Aleppo and Şems of Damascus opened Istanbul's first coffeehouse in Tahtakale in 1554, and UNESCO inscribed Turkish coffee culture in 2013 for the ritual rather than the bean: water first, a sweet alongside, grounds left in the cup for the fal. The cup is judged on the köpük, the fine foam, which comes from bringing the cezve up slowly and lifting it off as it rises, never letting it boil. Fazıl Bey's market-side Kadıköy counter does it properly at an everyday price. Turn the cup onto its saucer, let it cool, and in Kadıköy a falcı will read the grounds.
r-kahve.why: Judge the foam, then turn the cup over: the fal reading is the half of the ritual most visitors skip.
facts: Sade, az şekerli, orta or çok şekerli: sugar goes in before the boil, never after
Fazıl Bey'in Türk Kahvesi, Serasker Cad., Caferağa, Kadıköy; 0216 346 16 15
An even fine head across the whole cup; a flat one with a ring of scum was boiled
Drink the water first, do not stir, stop at the last centimetre; it closes a meal, it does not open one
Katina Fal Cafe, Pavlonya Sk. No:23/3, Kadıköy, +90 533 777 72 32, listed daily 11:30–21:00 on a site last dated 2013: phone first; readings in Turkish; agree the fee before the cup turns
Katina also advertises medyums: anything that grows into curse-lifting, paid follow-ups or a bank transfer is fraud, so stand up and leave
Sand-brewed kumda kahve is now mostly a visitor show; Şark Kahvesi in the Grand Bazaar (Zenneciler Sok.) has an unverified founding date and bazaar prices, and the bazaar shuts on Sundays
r-kahve.maps_query: Fazıl Bey'in Türk Kahvesi Kadıköy Istanbul

r-serpme.name: Serpme kahvaltı — the Sunday
r-serpme.teaser: Twenty plates, three hours, and nothing else planned for the day. It is an appointment, not a breakfast
r-serpme.story: Serpme kahvaltı works as a booking, not a meal you drop into. On Sunday from about ten until two the breakfast houses hold tables rather than turn them, and you make one decision per person: the egg. Menemen soft-scrambled with tomato and green pepper, sahanda fried in the pan, sucuklu with cured sausage, or a plain omelette. Then the plates land together and keep landing: bal kaymak, buffalo cream under comb honey, bread replaced hot, at least one plate you cannot name, and çay refilled before you notice the glass is empty. The Turkish coffee comes last, never first.
r-serpme.why: Do it once, on a Sunday, with nothing after: it is the most time-expensive pleasure in this fold.
facts: 'Serpme kahvaltı' and the number of people: the count is heads, not plates
Sunday about 10:00–14:00 is the institution; go at nine or at three to miss the eleven o'clock crush
Book, or be at the door when it opens
Per head on the board, so read the number as what one of you pays; the same house on a weekday costs a fraction
Van Kahvaltı Evi in Cihangir, Çakmak Kahvaltı Salonu on Beşiktaş's breakfast street, Emirgan Sütiş on the Bosphorus: each has its own card
No clearing as you go, no coffee at the start, nothing à la carte alongside the spread

r-raki-balik.name: Rakı-balık — choosing the fish off the ice
r-raki-balik.teaser: The fish is not on the menu. It is on ice by the door, priced by a kilo you have not yet asked about
r-raki-balik.story: The rakı table runs cold mezes, hot mezes, then one fish, and the fish is chosen, not ordered. You walk to the ice by the entrance, point, and it is weighed before it goes on the grill. That step is where visitors lose money most reliably in this city: the price is per kilo, the kilo price is often unposted, and a lüfer that looked like one dinner lands at nine hundred grams. Ask 'kilosu kaç?' before you point and ask to see the scale. Season decides the rest: palamut from September, lüfer peaking in October, hamsi through December.
r-raki-balik.why: Ask the kilo price before you point: a house that will not show it has already told you what it is.
facts: 'Kilosu kaç?' for the price per kilo; 'temizler misiniz?' to have it cleaned at a market counter
Fish in season; anything glossy and cheap in July is farmed or flown
Market counters in the morning, done by early afternoon; the rakı table in the evening, late
Kadıköy off Güneşlibahçe Sok., Beşiktaş Çarşı, Üsküdar Balıkçılar Çarşısı: fair prices, no rakı poured
Kumkapı has the worst name for the per-kilo trick; the Beyoğlu Balık Pazarı row is now more tables than market
Rakı first, cold water in so it clouds, ice last if at all; the water glass stays beside it and is drunk alongside
Moves weekly with the catch and the season: no fair figure can be printed
r-raki-balik.maps_query: Kadıköy Balık Pazarı Güneşlibahçe Sokak Istanbul

g-cinaralti.name: Çınaraltı, Çengelköy
g-cinaralti.teaser: Chairs set under a plane tree said to be nearly a thousand years old, on the Asian shore
g-cinaralti.story: The name means 'under the plane tree', and the tree is the whole proposition: a vast çınar on the Asian shore at Çengelköy, its canopy spread over tables that face the water. The garden pours tea and coffee and nothing else, and you are expected to bring your own food; people arrive with bags of it. There is no music, no backgammon, no nargile, and it keeps no closing hour. It is the least commercial room in this guide: you pay for the glass, and the shade and the Bosphorus come with it.
g-cinaralti.why: Bring a picnic and sit under the trunk: you pay for tea and nothing else.
facts: Tea and coffee only, by the glass
The near-thousand-year age of the tree is local telling, not a measured date

g-pierre-loti.name: Pierre Loti Kahvesi
g-pierre-loti.teaser: Tea on a hill above the graves, the whole Golden Horn laid out below, and a cable car to get up
g-pierre-loti.story: Evliya Çelebi knew this hill as the İdris Köşkü picnic ground. By the nineteenth century a coffeehouse called Rabia Kadın stood on it, and the French naval officer Julien Viaud, who wrote as Pierre Loti, arrived in 1876; he is said to have finished Aziyadé, published in 1879, at one of its tables. The hill took his name. Below the terrace lies Eyüp cemetery, long prized for its nearness to the tomb of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, over which Mehmed II raised a marble tomb and a mosque after 1453. Ride the cable car up; walk down through the graves.
g-pierre-loti.why: The descent on foot through the Ottoman cemetery is the reason to come, more than the tea.
facts: Teleferik from the Eyüp shore of the Golden Horn, about three minutes
Sunset, which is also the busiest
The walk back down through the cemetery
That Loti finished Aziyadé at this table is told, not documented

g-moda-aile.name: Moda Aile Çay Bahçesi
g-moda-aile.teaser: The whole of Kadıköy, three generations of it, facing the Marmara over a backgammon board
g-moda-aile.story: A municipal tea garden on the slope above Moda's shore: umbrellas and plastic chairs under tall trees, the Sea of Marmara filling the view and the Princes' Islands on the horizon. Nobody here is performing. Grandparents, students and dog-walkers hold tables for hours over tea and tavla, the clatter of the pieces carrying between the trees, the food runs to sandwiches and toast, and half the room brought its own. This is what the Asian side does with a free afternoon, and on a clear evening the islands go blue and then dark while nobody moves.
g-moda-aile.why: Come late in the afternoon and stay through the sunset, at municipal prices with the Marmara in front of you.
facts: Caferağa, Park İçi Yolu, Moda, Kadıköy
Outdoor only, so the weather decides
Tea, with a sandwich or toast, or bring your own
The Princes' Islands on the horizon as the light goes
g-moda-aile.maps_query: Moda Aile Çay Bahçesi Kadıköy Istanbul

g-inci.name: İnci Pastanesi
g-inci.teaser: One dessert, one recipe, since the 1940s, and a redevelopment that moved the whole shop round the corner
g-inci.story: İnci opened in the Cercle d'Orient building on İstiklal in the mid-1940s and built its name on a single plate: the profiterol, choux balls filled with pastry cream under a pour of dark chocolate sauce. It is the version every other in the country is measured against. When the building was redeveloped in the early 2010s the shop was evicted, went dark for about seventy days, and reopened round the corner on Mis Sokak with the recipe unchanged. The room is new; the plate is the old one, and that is the only reason to come.
g-inci.why: Order the profiterol and nothing else: it is the benchmark for the whole country.
facts: The chocolate sauce: it is the recipe, more than the choux
g-inci.maps_query: İnci Pastanesi Mis Sokak Beyoğlu Istanbul

g-markiz.name: Markiz (ex-Lebon)
g-markiz.teaser: Four Art Nouveau seasons were ordered from France; two of them are still on the wall
g-markiz.story: Lebon's patisserie traded on the Grand Rue from the 1880s and became the salon of Pera, with Pierre Loti and the poet Yahya Kemal among its regulars. Its Art Nouveau faience panels were ordered from France: four seasons were commissioned, and only Spring and Autumn hang in the room today. When Lebon moved across the street in 1940, Avedis Ohanyan Çakır opened Markiz in the space it left and kept the tiles. It closed in 1980 and came back, panels and all, in 2003. Take a table that faces the walls.
g-markiz.why: You pay grand-café prices to sit with the two surviving seasons of Pera's old salon.
facts: İstiklal Cad. 360–362, Beyoğlu, at the corner of the Oriental passage
The Spring and Autumn faience panels

g-kronotrop.name: Kronotrop, Cihangir
g-kronotrop.teaser: Sixteen and a half hours a day of table, on the Cihangir slope above Tophane
g-kronotrop.story: Kronotrop opened in 2012 as one of Turkey's first specialty roasteries; its founder, Çağatay Gülabioğlu, was the country's first Q grader. The Cihangir room is the flagship, on the slope above Tophane where many of the city's writers, editors and film people live, and it keeps the longest hours of any desk on this list, from seven in the morning to half past eleven at night. It is small and it fills, so the etiquette is one long session, not a whole day at the same table. The chain has passed forty branches with very different hours: aim for this one.
g-kronotrop.why: The early start and late close make it the one counter that fits round a crew's shifts.
facts: One long session, then give up the table
Beans roasted by the house, by the bag

g-montag.name: Montag Coffee Roasters
g-montag.teaser: The roaster most of the scene credits as the pioneer, and the Kadıköy room is where you sit
g-montag.story: Montag has roasted its own beans since 2016, and much of the city's specialty scene credits it as the pioneer. It runs rooms in Kadıköy, Moda and Bomonti, and the Kadıköy one on Muvakkıthane Caddesi is where you sit down: counter downstairs, a quiet upper floor, V60 and cold brew alongside espresso. The turnover is quick enough that the bag you buy was roasted recently, which matters if you are provisioning before a passage. The upstairs room is the working one, and Baylan sits at number 9 on the same street when you need a break.
g-montag.why: Buy beans here before a passage: the turnover keeps the bags fresh.
facts: Caferağa, Muvakkıthane Cad. No:16/A, first floor, Kadıköy
A V60 or cold brew, upstairs
g-montag.maps_query: Montag Coffee Roasters Muvakkıthane Kadıköy Istanbul

g-petra.name: Petra Roasting Co., Bebek
g-petra.teaser: Where the shore walk ends and the morning's work starts, from half past seven
g-petra.story: The walk north from Arnavutköy along the water, past the wooden yalı, ends in Bebek, and Petra's Bebek branch opens at half past seven on weekdays: the obvious place to set a laptop down after the best early hour on the European shore. It is closed on Mondays, so build the walk around a Tuesday. If you are on the wrong side of the hill there are branches at Gayrettepe, Şişhane, Topağacı and Maslak; the Şişhane one also closes Mondays, the others do not. Weekends start later, at ten.
g-petra.why: Walk the shore from Arnavutköy first, then work here with the morning already done.
facts: The Arnavutköy to Bebek shore walk before it

g-ataturk.name: Atatürk Kitaplığı
g-ataturk.teaser: Eldem's 1970s library above Taksim: a research collection now, no longer an open reading room
g-ataturk.story: Sedad Hakkı Eldem, the architect who spent a career folding the Ottoman timber house into modernism, drew a culture complex here of library, museum and exhibition halls; only the library was built. Koç Holding raised it in 1973 and the collection moved in on 3 March 1981: around 228,000 books, 20,000 periodicals and 10,000 bound volumes of newspapers, with manuscripts, maps, albums and postcards. Since 5 September 2022 the city has run it as a research library: researchers are admitted, and general readers and students are sent to İBB's Sevgi Soysal library nearby. Come for the building and the archive, not a free desk.
g-ataturk.why: For a researcher, the city's Ottoman maps, albums and postcards under one Eldem roof.
facts: Gümüşsuyu, Miralay Şefikbey Sok. No:6, Beyoğlu
To researchers; hours not re-confirmed since the change, ask İBB before you go (Oct 2026)
General readers go to İBB's Sevgi Soysal library instead
Eldem's building itself, seen from the street

g-salt.name: SALT Galata
g-salt.teaser: The Imperial Ottoman Bank's head office, emptied of money and handed to readers for nothing
g-salt.story: Alexandre Vallaury built this as the Imperial Ottoman Bank's headquarters, finished in 1892, and the bank worked from it until 1999. Han Tümertekin's conversion reopened it in November 2011 as SALT Galata: galleries, a street-level café and bookshop, and the bank's own archive covering 145 years. Reading costs nothing. The open library is for everyone; the Ferit F. Şahenk study hall takes registered researchers with a personal pass, in bookable blocks of up to three hours, and nothing circulates. Outside, the Camondo Stairs, cut around 1870 to 1880 by the banker Abraham Salomon Camondo, still climb the hill.
g-salt.why: A free, quiet desk inside a banking palace, with the Camondo Stairs a minute from the door.
facts: SALT Research Tue–Sat 11:00–19:00; galleries Tue–Sat 12:00–20:00, Sun 12:00–18:00 per Time Out; closed Mondays and on Eid and national holidays (Oct 2026)
Register at saltresearch.org for the study hall
Much of the archive is digitised and searchable at saltresearch.org
Neolokal, Maksut Aşkar's MICHELIN-starred room, in the same building
The Camondo Stairs, a minute's walk
g-salt.maps_query: SALT Galata Bankalar Caddesi Karaköy Istanbul

sources.label: Salt: Salt Research Ferit F. Şahenk Hall

g-yildiz.name: Çadır Köşkü, Yıldız Park
g-yildiz.teaser: A sultan's walled garden, two pavilions turned cafés, and a glass of çay under the trees
g-yildiz.story: Abdülhamid II walled the outer garden of Yıldız Palace and filled it with artificial lakes, summer houses and a porcelain factory that still works. Two of those pavilions, Çadır and Malta, now serve breakfast, lunch or a glass of tea under the trees, inside what has become a public park of some 368,000 square metres, run with the park's other restaurants by the municipal operator BELTUR. The honest work truth: the climb from the Beşiktaş gate is steep enough that nobody arrives wanting to open a laptop. Leave it on board and come for the trees.
g-yildiz.why: Come for the sultan's garden and a slow breakfast, not for a working day.
facts: Yıldız Park, Beşiktaş: the Çadır and Malta pavilions
On foot, uphill, from the Beşiktaş gate
Breakfast, lunch, or tea under the trees
Not a place for it: the climb argues you out of the laptop
The porcelain factory, still working inside the park walls
g-yildiz.maps_query: Çadır Köşkü Yıldız Parkı Beşiktaş Istanbul
